name: eiffelstudio
desc: Development environment for the Eiffel language
why: Design-by-contract Eiffel is a genuinely unusual object-oriented lineage, and its full IDE is a door into a world most developers never visited.

brief.what_it_is: EiffelStudio is a commercial integrated development environment for the Eiffel programming language, published by Eiffel Software. The homepage presents it as a tool for building software whose behavior is defined and enforced, centered on Design by Contract: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants that are part of the language, checked automatically, and understood by the tools. The pages read do not describe concrete inputs or outputs beyond Eiffel source code going through the IDE. The Homebrew metadata lists the executables ec, ecb, estudio, compile_all, finish_freezing, iron, syntax_updater, and vision2_demo, but the pages read do not explain them.
brief.why_it_exists: The site argues that conventional tools optimize for coding speed and rely on testing to catch errors late, leaving assumptions implicit and contracts informal. EiffelStudio is pitched as a way to make correctness explicit, executable, and continuously enforced.
brief.how_it_works: The pages describe Design by Contract as the core mechanism: preconditions state what a component requires, postconditions state what it guarantees, and invariants state what must always hold. Violations are reported at the point of failure. The homepage also claims automatic testing that needs no test cases or oracles, and it mentions SCOOP for concurrency, but the pages read do not explain how either works.
brief.install_notes: Nothing about installation was visible on the pages read. The site has Downloads, System Requirements, Licensing, and Purchase sections, and the product offers a Try option alongside Buy, but I did not open those pages. The Homebrew formula's caveats field is empty.
brief.standout: Design by Contract is a long-standing object-oriented method that most mainstream IDEs do not build around, and the site claims the IDE uses contracts for navigation and testing. The automatic-testing claim, that there are no test cases and no test oracles, is unusual, but it is a vendor claim that I could not verify from these pages.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the pages show. The news section lists EiffelStudio 25.12 as the newest item, followed by 25.02 and 24.05, and the site is actively run. I saw no release dates or repository commit history, so this is a judgment from the vendor site, not a verified release cadence.
brief.caveats: This is a commercial product with a Purchase page and Enterprise tier, so it is not free software. The homepage is heavy marketing, and its claims about correctness and automatic testing are not backed by anything I read. I did not open the Licensing or System Requirements pages, so platform support and license terms are unverified. The executables list comes from the Homebrew package metadata, not from any README or doc page.
quotes: It is built around a single principle: correctness must be explicit, executable, and continuously enforced.
Testing validates samples of behavior. It does not define what must never happen.
fetch_log: https://www.eiffel.com (worked; marketing homepage, no README or install commands)
https://www.eiffel.com/downloads/ (worked; a guessed URL, and it returned the EiffelStudio product overview with Design by Contract details and testimonials, but no install instructions)

judge.reason: Eiffel makes preconditions, postconditions, and invariants executable parts of programming, offering a distinctive language and IDE built around correctness rather than another generic development tool.

entry.title: EiffelStudio
entry.tldr: A full IDE for Eiffel, the object-oriented language where preconditions, postconditions and invariants are part of the code itself.
entry.deeper_look:
EiffelStudio is the development environment for Eiffel, published by Eiffel Software. Eiffel is built around Design by Contract: each routine states what it requires (preconditions) and what it guarantees (postconditions), and each class states what must always hold (invariants). These are written in the language and checked automatically, and violations are reported at the point of failure.

The site's argument is that most tooling optimizes for writing code quickly and leaves assumptions implicit, then relies on testing to catch problems late. In its words: "Testing validates samples of behavior. It does not define what must never happen." The project is pitched as a way to make correctness "explicit, executable, and continuously enforced."

The homepage also mentions automatic testing that needs no test cases or oracles, and SCOOP for concurrency. The pages read do not explain how either works, and the testing claim is a vendor claim, so treat it as something to check yourself.

Homebrew installs several executables: ec, ecb, estudio, compile_all, finish_freezing, iron, syntax_updater and vision2_demo. The pages read do not describe them, so the names are all this entry can offer. The GTK3 dependencies suggest estudio is the graphical IDE and vision2_demo a toolkit demo, but that is a guess from the names.
entry.install:
brew install eiffelstudio
# pulls in GTK+3 and related libraries for the graphical IDE

try_this.what_happens: Prints usage for ec, which is listed as an installed executable; its role is not explained in the pages read.
Shows options for the estudio executable, which is likely the graphical IDE.

entry.whats_unique: Design by Contract is built into the language and, per the site, into the IDE's navigation and testing, rather than added through a library or a linter.
entry.caveats: The vendor sells it commercially with Purchase and Enterprise tiers, the homepage is mostly marketing, and licensing terms and platform support were not verified; the Homebrew formula lists GPL-2.0-only.
